name: Mars Pathfinder
keyDiscovery: Mars Pathfinder proved that low-cost airbag landings work on Mars and that a small rover could navigate and analyse rocks on another planet.
missionLegacy: Pathfinder and Sojourner revived public excitement for Mars exploration after a 20-year gap and proved the 'faster, better, cheaper' approach could succeed, leading directly to the MER rovers.
funFact: Sojourner weighed just 10.6 kg — about the same as a medium-sized dog — and was the first wheeled vehicle to drive on another planet.
heritageNote: The Carl Sagan Memorial Station and Sojourner rover remain at Ares Vallis, silent since September 1997; they are among the most historically significant robotic exploration sites on Mars.

objects.name: Pathfinder Base Station
objects.description: The Mars Pathfinder base station, later named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station, was a low-cost lander that demonstrated a new airbag landing system. It bounced 15 times on the surface before coming to rest. The station served as a communications relay and carried the IMP camera and atmospheric instruments.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Demonstrated the first airbag landing system on Mars and served as a relay station transmitting 2.3 gigabits of data including 16,500 images.
objects.legacy: Renamed the Carl Sagan Memorial Station, it sits with petals open at Ares Vallis, undisturbed since losing contact in September 1997.
objects.firstPerson: I bounced fifteen times across Mars before I finally stopped. Then I opened my petals like a flower, rolled out my ramp, and let little Sojourner drive out onto a new world. For 83 days we worked together — I relayed everything home. Now I sit named after Carl Sagan, a monument to curiosity.

objects.name: Sojourner Rover
objects.description: Sojourner was the first rover to operate on another planet. Weighing just 10.6 kg (about the size of a microwave oven), it explored about 100 square metres of the surface over 83 sols. Sojourner carried an Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer to analyse rock compositions, finding that some rocks were similar to Earth's andesite.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Performed the first rover-based chemical analysis of Martian rocks, revealing unexpectedly silicon-rich compositions similar to Earth's andesite.
objects.legacy: Sojourner last communicated on 27 September 1997; it likely sits within a few metres of the base station, its solar panels long covered in dust.
objects.firstPerson: I was the first rover ever to drive on another planet. I was tiny — no bigger than a microwave — but I was brave. For 83 Martian days I nosed up to rocks, tasted them with my spectrometer, and showed the world that a little robot could explore another world. Every Mars rover after me started with my tracks.

objects.name: Deployment Ramp
objects.description: After landing and deflating its airbags, Pathfinder opened its petals and deployed two ramps for Sojourner to drive down. The rear ramp was blocked by a partially deflated airbag, so engineers commanded Sojourner to use the front ramp. This was the first time a rover drove onto the surface of another planet.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Enabled the historic moment when Sojourner became the first wheeled vehicle to drive onto the surface of another planet.
objects.legacy: The ramps remain attached to the open petals of the base station, frozen in the position that launched interplanetary roving.
objects.firstPerson: I was just a ramp — two metal tracks folded against a lander. But on 6 July 1997, little Sojourner rolled down me and touched Martian soil for the first time. That made me the bridge between two worlds. My rear twin was blocked by a stubborn airbag, so I got the honour all to myself.

objects.name: IMP Camera Mast
objects.description: The Imager for Mars Pathfinder (IMP) was a stereo camera mounted on a 1.5-metre mast. It captured over 16,500 images of the Martian landscape and provided the first 360-degree colour panoramas from Mars since Viking. The camera had 12 geology filters and 12 atmospheric filters for scientific analysis.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Captured over 16,500 images with 24 spectral filters, producing the first 360-degree colour panoramas of Mars since Viking 21 years earlier.
objects.legacy: The IMP mast still rises 1.5 metres above the base station, pointing at a Martian horizon it can no longer photograph.
objects.firstPerson: From my perch 1.5 metres up, I saw Mars in a way no camera had for twenty years. I snapped 16,500 pictures — sunsets, dust devils, Sojourner posing next to rocks. My panoramas showed the whole world what a Martian afternoon looks like. I had 24 different filters, one for every question scientists wanted to ask.

objects.name: Barnacle Bill Rock
objects.description: The first rock analysed by Sojourner's APXS instrument was informally named 'Barnacle Bill'. Analysis revealed it was rich in silicon, similar to andesite found on Earth. This was surprising — scientists expected basaltic compositions. It suggested Mars had a more complex geological history than previously thought.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Revealed a silicon-rich andesitic composition that overturned the assumption Mars had only simple basaltic geology, proving a more complex volcanic history.
objects.legacy: Barnacle Bill still sits where Sojourner analysed it, an ordinary-looking rock that changed our understanding of Martian geology.
objects.firstPerson: I am just a rock, but I was the first rock on Mars that a rover ever touched. When Sojourner pressed her spectrometer against me, scientists gasped — I was not what they expected. I am rich in silicon, like volcanic rocks on Earth. I proved that Mars has a far more complex history than anyone guessed.

objects.name: Yogi Rock
objects.description: Yogi was a large rock near the Pathfinder landing site, about one metre tall. Sojourner spent several sols driving to and analysing Yogi. APXS measurements showed it had a basaltic composition, different from Barnacle Bill, indicating variety in the local geology. Wind-sculpted features on its surface showed evidence of aeolian erosion.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Showed a basaltic composition contrasting with nearby Barnacle Bill, proving geological diversity exists within metres on the Martian surface.
objects.legacy: Yogi remains at Ares Vallis, its wind-sculpted face slowly being reshaped by Martian dust storms over the decades.
objects.firstPerson: I am Yogi, a boulder the size of a bear, and I told a different story from my neighbour Barnacle Bill. Where Bill was silicon-rich, I am plain basalt — proof that Mars mixes its rocks like Earth does. The wind has been sculpting my face for millions of years, and Sojourner was the first to notice.
